title: Present Perfect vs. Present Perfect Continuous
subtitle: Know when to focus on the result, and when to focus on the activity itself.
objectives: Choose between the two tenses based on what you want to emphasize
Use the simple form for completed, countable achievements
Use the continuous form for ongoing duration or an uncompleted, repeated activity

content.intro: Both tenses connect the past to now — the real skill is choosing which one fits what you actually want to say.

rules.heading: Present perfect (simple) — result, completion, quantity
rules.body:
• I have read three books this month. (a completed, countable result)
  • She has cleaned the kitchen. (it's done, look at the result)

rules.heading: Present perfect continuous — activity, duration, ongoing
rules.body:
• I have been reading this book for two weeks. (still not finished, emphasizing the activity/duration)
  • She has been cleaning the kitchen all morning. (the process itself, maybe not even finished)

examples: I have written three emails this morning. (completed, countable)
I have been writing emails all morning. (the activity, ongoing feel)
She has been reading that book for a week. (in progress)
He has painted the fence. (done, result visible)
He has been painting the fence since 9am. (still going, or just stopped)

commonMistakes.wrong: I have been reading three books this month. (a completed count)
commonMistakes.right: I have read three books this month.
commonMistakes.why: A specific, completed quantity needs the present perfect simple, not the continuous.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have written this email for twenty minutes. (still writing)
commonMistakes.right: I have been writing this email for twenty minutes.
commonMistakes.why: Ongoing duration of an unfinished activity needs the continuous form.

commonMistakes.wrong: She has been finished the report.
commonMistakes.why: "Finish" describing a completed result uses the simple form, not "has been finished" (which also isn't grammatically correct as written).

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Choose the present perfect simple or continuous, depending on the emphasis.

items.prompt: I ___ (write) three emails this morning. (a completed count)
items.explanation: A specific, countable, completed result — present perfect simple.

items.prompt: I ___ (write) emails all morning. (the ongoing activity)
items.explanation: Emphasis on the activity and its duration — present perfect continuous.
A completed action — present perfect simple.

items.prompt: She ___ (read) that book for a week now. (still going)
items.explanation: Ongoing, unfinished duration — present perfect continuous.

items.prompt: How many cups of coffee ___ today?
items.explanation: "How many" asks for a countable result — present perfect simple.
A visible result of a recent, ongoing-feeling activity — present perfect continuous.

items.incorrect: I have been finishing my homework. (it's done)
items.explanation: A completed result needs the simple form, not the continuous.

items.incorrect: He has painted the fence for three hours. (still not done)
answer: He has been painting the fence for three hours.
items.explanation: Ongoing duration needs the continuous form.

summary: Present perfect simple = result, completion, a countable quantity.
Present perfect continuous = the activity itself, duration, possibly still ongoing.
Ask yourself: am I emphasizing what's done, or how long/how much activity happened?
